title: CTS Practical Theology — Unit 9: Self-Control and the Besetting Sin

blocks.en: 🌱 Practical Theology — Unit 9: Self-Control and the Besetting Sin
blocks.es_reference: 🌱 Teología Práctica — Unidad 9: El Dominio Propio y el Pecado Dominante

blocks.en: Professors: Dr. Wayne Cook & Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesores: Dr. Wayne Cook y Dr. Ted Rogers
Introducción

blocks.en: Salvation is the free gift of God, received by faith and never earned. Yet the believer who has been saved still carries the flesh, which wars against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17) — not a second person living inside him, but the continuing pull of sin's power in a life now indwelt by the Spirit and made new in Christ. We are not saved by self-control, but we are saved into a life of self-control, for the Spirit who lives in us produces it. This unit takes up two related truths: the grace of self-control, which God grows in us, and the besetting sin, the particular weakness that so easily trips each of us. The goal is not to earn God's favor by mastering ourselves, but to walk out the grace already given, letting the Spirit win the daily battle.
blocks.es_reference: La salvación es el don gratuito de Dios, recibido por la fe y jamás ganado. Sin embargo, el creyente que ha sido salvo todavía lleva la carne, que lucha contra el Espíritu (Gálatas 5:17) — no una segunda persona que vive dentro de él, sino la fuerza continua del pecado en una vida ahora habitada por el Espíritu y hecha nueva en Cristo. No somos salvos por el dominio propio, pero sí somos salvos a una vida de dominio propio, porque el Espíritu que vive en nosotros lo produce. Esta unidad trata dos verdades relacionadas: la gracia del dominio propio, que Dios hace crecer en nosotros, y el pecado dominante, la debilidad particular que tan fácilmente nos hace tropezar a cada uno. La meta no es ganar el favor de Dios dominándonos a nosotros mismos, sino vivir la gracia ya dada, dejando que el Espíritu gane la batalla diaria.

blocks.en: I. Self-Control Is a Fruit of the Spirit
blocks.es_reference: I. El Dominio Propio Es Fruto del Espíritu

blocks.en: Self-control is not first a matter of gritted teeth and iron willpower; it is fruit. Paul writes, "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Against such there is no law" (Galatians 5:22–23, NKJV). Fruit grows from a living root; it is produced by the Spirit in the believer, not manufactured by the flesh. This is why an unbeliever, however disciplined, cannot produce this fruit, and why the believer must lean on the Spirit and not merely on resolve. We do work and we do strive — but we strive in the strength the Spirit supplies, looking to Him for the power we do not have in ourselves.
blocks.es_reference: El dominio propio no es ante todo cuestión de dientes apretados y fuerza de voluntad de hierro; es fruto. Pablo escribe: "Mas el fruto del Espíritu es amor, gozo, paz, paciencia, benignidad, bondad, fe, mansedumbre, templanza; contra tales cosas no hay ley" (Gálatas 5:22–23, RVG). Templanza, es decir, dominio propio. El fruto crece de una raíz viva; lo produce el Espíritu en el creyente, no lo fabrica la carne. Por eso un incrédulo, por disciplinado que sea, no puede producir este fruto, y por eso el creyente debe apoyarse en el Espíritu y no solo en su resolución. Sí trabajamos y sí nos esforzamos — pero nos esforzamos en la fuerza que el Espíritu provee, mirándole a Él por el poder que no tenemos en nosotros mismos.
II. El Pecado Dominante

blocks.en: Every believer carries some particular weakness that trips him more than others — what older writers called the besetting sin. "Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which so easily ensnares us, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us" (Hebrews 12:1, NKJV). For one it is anger; for another it is lust, or pride, or fear, or the tongue, or strong drink, or laziness. The first step is honesty: to name it before God rather than excuse it. Solomon warns what happens when a man has no command over himself: "Whoever has no rule over his own spirit is like a city broken down, without walls" (Proverbs 25:28, NKJV). A city without walls lies open to every enemy; so does a heart without self-control.
blocks.es_reference: Cada creyente lleva alguna debilidad particular que lo hace tropezar más que otras — lo que los autores antiguos llamaban el pecado dominante. "Despojémonos de todo peso y del pecado que nos asedia, y corramos con paciencia la carrera que tenemos por delante" (Hebreos 12:1, RVG). Para uno es la ira; para otro es la lujuria, o el orgullo, o el temor, o la lengua, o la bebida, o la pereza. El primer paso es la honestidad: nombrarlo delante de Dios en vez de excusarlo. Salomón advierte lo que sucede cuando un hombre no se domina: "Como ciudad derribada y sin muro, es el hombre cuyo espíritu no tiene rienda" (Proverbios 25:28, RVG). Una ciudad sin muros queda expuesta a todo enemigo; así también un corazón sin dominio propio.
III. Una Mirada Más Cercana: la Ira

blocks.en: Anger is perhaps the most common besetting sin, so the Scriptures give it special attention. Anger itself is not always sin — God Himself is angry at evil — but it turns to sin quickly: "'Be angry, and do not sin': do not let the sun go down on your wrath, nor give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:26–27, NKJV). James shows the path of wisdom: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath; for the wrath of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:19–20, NKJV). From the Scriptures we can draw simple, God-given helps. First, a gentle answer: "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1, NKJV) — Abigail's calm, careful words turned David away from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25). Second, a holy delay — be slow to speak, giving the heart time to cool before the mouth opens. Third, the grace to overlook: "The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger, and his glory is to overlook a transgression" (Proverbs 19:11, NKJV) — David spared Saul again and again, refusing to repay insult for insult (1 Samuel 24). Not every offense must be answered; much of peace is learning what to let pass.
blocks.es_reference: La ira es quizá el pecado dominante más común, por eso las Escrituras le prestan especial atención. La ira en sí no siempre es pecado — Dios mismo se aíra contra el mal — pero pronto se vuelve pecado: "Airaos, y no pequéis; no se ponga el sol sobre vuestro enojo; ni deis lugar al diablo" (Efesios 4:26–27, RVG). Santiago muestra el camino de la sabiduría: "todo hombre sea pronto para oír, tardo para hablar, tardo para airarse; porque la ira del hombre no obra la justicia de Dios" (Santiago 1:19–20, RVG). De las Escrituras podemos sacar ayudas sencillas dadas por Dios. Primera, una respuesta blanda: "La blanda respuesta quita la ira; mas la palabra áspera hace subir el furor" (Proverbios 15:1, RVG) — las palabras serenas y prudentes de Abigail apartaron a David del derramamiento de sangre (1 Samuel 25). Segunda, una demora santa — ser tardo para hablar, dando al corazón tiempo de enfriarse antes de que se abra la boca. Tercera, la gracia de disimular: "La cordura del hombre detiene su furor; y su honra es disimular la ofensa" (Proverbios 19:11, RVG) — David perdonó a Saúl una y otra vez, negándose a pagar insulto por insulto (1 Samuel 24). No toda ofensa debe ser respondida; gran parte de la paz consiste en aprender qué dejar pasar.
IV. Hacer Morir el Pecado

blocks.en: Self-control is not only resisting; it is also putting sin to death at the root. "For if you live according to the flesh you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13, NKJV). Notice that it is by the Spirit that we put sin to death — not by the flesh's own willpower. Paul commands the same: "Therefore put to death your members which are on the earth" (Colossians 3:5, NKJV). And sometimes the wisest battle is flight rather than a fair fight: "Flee also youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace" (2 Timothy 2:22, NKJV). We starve the besetting sin and feed the new life.
blocks.es_reference: El dominio propio no es solo resistir; es también hacer morir el pecado de raíz. "Porque si vivís conforme a la carne, moriréis; mas si por el Espíritu hacéis morir las obras de la carne, viviréis" (Romanos 8:13, RVG). Note que es por el Espíritu que hacemos morir el pecado — no por la fuerza de voluntad de la carne. Pablo manda lo mismo: "Haced morir, pues, vuestros miembros que están sobre la tierra" (Colosenses 3:5, RVG). Y a veces la batalla más sabia es huir en vez de pelear de frente: "Huye también de los deseos juveniles; y sigue la justicia, la fe, el amor, la paz" (2 Timoteo 2:22, RVG). Matamos de hambre al pecado dominante y alimentamos la nueva vida.
V. Andar en el Espíritu

blocks.en: How then do we win? Not by trying harder in our own strength, but by walking in step with the Spirit. "I say then: Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16, NKJV). There is a real war inside the believer: "For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another" (Galatians 5:17, NKJV). Victory does not come by pretending the flesh is already dead, nor by fighting it with the flesh's own weapons, but by yielding to the Spirit moment by moment. We are responsible to walk; the power to walk is His.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Cómo, pues, vencemos? No esforzándonos más en nuestras propias fuerzas, sino andando al paso del Espíritu. "Digo, pues: Andad en el Espíritu, y no satisfagáis los deseos de la carne" (Gálatas 5:16, RVG). Hay una guerra real dentro del creyente: "Porque la carne codicia contra el Espíritu, y el Espíritu contra la carne; y éstos se oponen entre sí" (Gálatas 5:17, RVG). La victoria no viene fingiendo que la carne ya está muerta, ni peleando contra ella con las armas de la misma carne, sino cediendo al Espíritu momento a momento. Somos responsables de andar; el poder para andar es suyo.
Conclusión

blocks.en: The disciplined life is not a way to earn God's acceptance — that was settled at the cross and is received by faith. It is the way a saved person lives out the grace already given, letting the Spirit master what we cannot master alone. Name your besetting sin honestly. Bring it daily to the Lord. Lean on the Spirit, who alone produces the fruit of self-control. A heart ruled by the Spirit is a city with strong walls — and the grace that saved you is more than enough to keep you.
blocks.es_reference: La vida disciplinada no es un medio para ganar la aceptación de Dios — eso quedó resuelto en la cruz y se recibe por la fe. Es la manera en que una persona salva vive la gracia ya dada, dejando que el Espíritu domine lo que no podemos dominar solos. Nombre su pecado dominante con honestidad. Llévelo cada día al Señor. Apóyese en el Espíritu, el único que produce el fruto del dominio propio. Un corazón gobernado por el Espíritu es una ciudad de muros fuertes — y la gracia que lo salvó es más que suficiente para guardarlo.

mc.stem: What does this unit teach about salvation and the disciplined life of self-control?
options: We are saved by mastering ourselves through strict self-control
We are saved by grace through faith, never by self-control; the disciplined life flows out of salvation and does not earn it
Self-control earns God's acceptance little by little
The disciplined life removes our need for grace

mc.stem: According to Galatians 5:22-23, self-control is...
options: A work of the flesh achieved by sheer willpower
Something unnecessary for those who have faith
A reward given only to pastors and leaders
A fruit of the Spirit, produced in the believer by the Holy Spirit

mc.stem: Why does the unit say even a disciplined unbeliever cannot produce this fruit?
options: Because unbelievers are simply not trying hard enough
Because this fruit was only for the Old Testament saints
Because the fruit is produced by the indwelling Spirit, whom the unbeliever does not have
Because self-control is impossible for any human being

mc.stem: What does Hebrews 12:1 call the particular sin that trips each believer?
options: The sin which so easily ensnares us, which we must lay aside as we run the race
A sin that no true Christian ever commits
A sin that troubles only unbelievers
An unforgivable sin

mc.stem: In Proverbs 25:28, a man who has no rule over his own spirit is like...
options: A strong tower that can never fall
A city broken down, without walls
A well-watered garden in summer
A ship safely anchored in harbor

mc.stem: What does Ephesians 4:26-27 teach about anger?
options: 'Be angry, and do not sin'; do not let the sun go down on your wrath, nor give place to the devil
That anger is always sin and must never even be felt
That anger should always be expressed loudly and immediately
That true believers will never feel any anger

mc.stem: According to James 1:19-20, every person should be...
options: Quick to speak and quick to become angry
Slow to listen and eager to argue
Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath, for man's wrath does not produce God's righteousness
Silent at all times to avoid all conflict

mc.stem: What does Proverbs 15:1 say turns away wrath?
options: A loud and forceful reply
Complete silence and withdrawal
Winning the argument with strong words
A soft, gentle answer, while a harsh word stirs up anger

mc.stem: In the unit's example, how did Abigail turn David away from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25)?
options: By raising an army against him
With calm, careful, humble words - a prepared gentle answer
By matching his anger with her own
By ignoring him until he gave up

mc.stem: What is the second God-given help for anger named in this unit?
options: Demanding an immediate apology
Telling everyone about the offense
Repaying the insult in kind
A holy delay - being slow to speak, giving the heart time to cool

mc.stem: According to Proverbs 19:11, what is a man's glory?
options: To overlook a transgression, being slow to anger
To punish every wrong done to him
To win every argument
To remember every offense against him

mc.stem: How does David sparing Saul (1 Samuel 24) illustrate self-control?
options: He took revenge when he had the chance
He demanded a public apology from Saul
He refused to repay insult for insult, overlooking the offense for God's sake
He fled the country to avoid the problem

mc.stem: According to Romans 8:13, how do we put the deeds of the body to death?
options: By the Spirit - not by the flesh's own willpower
By making a public vow once a year
By comparing ourselves to worse sinners
By ignoring sin until it goes away

mc.stem: What does Colossians 3:5 command believers to do?
options: To excuse the sins of the flesh as harmless
To keep their sin a private secret forever
To wait passively for sin to disappear on its own
To put to death their members which are on the earth

mc.stem: What does 2 Timothy 2:22 say is sometimes the wisest battle?
options: To argue the temptation down
To prove we are strong by staying near it
To flee youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace
To give in once so the desire will fade

mc.stem: What does Galatians 5:16 promise to those who walk in the Spirit?
options: That they will never be tempted again
That they shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh
That they will no longer need the Scriptures
That they will become sinlessly perfect at once

mc.stem: What does Galatians 5:17 say about the flesh and the Spirit?
options: The Spirit always loses to the flesh
They are at perfect peace within the believer
The flesh has already been destroyed entirely
They war against each other and are contrary to one another within the believer

mc.stem: According to the unit, how is victory over the flesh actually won?
options: By yielding to the Spirit moment by moment, walking in step with Him
By trying harder in our own strength
By pretending the flesh no longer exists
By fighting the flesh with the flesh's own weapons

mc.stem: What does the unit say is the first step in dealing with a besetting sin?
options: Hiding it carefully from God and others
Deciding it is too strong to ever change
Honesty - naming it before God rather than excusing it
Waiting until it stops bothering us

mc.stem: What is the proper foundation and motive for the whole disciplined life of self-control?
options: Fear that God will reject us if we fail
The grace of God in Christ - living out the salvation already given, by the Spirit's power
Earning God's acceptance by mastering ourselves
A wish to look holier than other people

sa.prompt: Why does this unit say self-control is more than human willpower? Use Galatians 5.
sa.model: Paul writes that self-control is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23), meaning it is produced by the Spirit living in the believer, not manufactured by the flesh through gritted teeth and willpower alone. This is why an unbeliever, however disciplined, cannot produce this fruit; the believer must depend on and walk by the Spirit's power, not merely on human resolve.

sa.prompt: What is a 'besetting sin,' and what does Hebrews 12:1 tell us to do with it?
sa.model: A besetting sin is the particular weakness that trips a believer more easily than others — anger, lust, pride, fear, or any recurring sin. Hebrews 12:1 tells us to lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily ensnares us, and to run with endurance the race set before us, treating the besetting sin as something to actively strip off, not something to excuse or carry along.

sa.prompt: How does Ephesians 4:26-27 guide a believer in handling anger?
sa.model: Ephesians 4:26-27 says, 'Be angry, and do not sin: do not let the sun go down on your wrath, nor give place to the devil.' It teaches that anger itself is not automatically sin, but it turns to sin quickly if nursed — so the believer must deal with anger promptly, before nightfall, so it does not become a foothold for the devil.

sa.prompt: Name the three Scripture-anchored helps for anger taught in this unit.
sa.model: The three Scripture-anchored helps for anger taught in this unit are: a gentle answer, since a soft answer turns away wrath while a harsh word stirs up anger (Proverbs 15:1); a holy delay, being slow to speak so the heart cools before the mouth opens; and the grace to overlook an offense rather than answering every insult (Proverbs 19:11).

sa.prompt: What does James 1:19-20 teach about being swift, slow, and the wrath of man?
sa.model: James 1:19-20 teaches that every man should be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath, for the wrath of man does not produce the righteousness of God. It reverses our natural instinct — quick to talk and quick to anger — and calls us instead to listen first and let anger cool, since human anger does not accomplish what God desires.

sa.prompt: What do Romans 8:13 and Colossians 3:5 mean by putting sin to death, and by whose power?
sa.model: Romans 8:13 and Colossians 3:5 mean putting sin to death at the root — not merely resisting it but actively killing its power in our members. Both make clear this is done by the Spirit's power, not the flesh's own willpower: 'if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live' (Romans 8:13).

sa.prompt: What does Galatians 5:16 promise about walking in the Spirit?
sa.model: Galatians 5:16 promises, 'Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.' Walking in step with the Spirit, moment by moment, is the way victory over sinful desire is won — not by trying harder in our own strength, but by yielding to the Spirit's leading.

sa.prompt: Why can we not win over a besetting sin by our own self-effort alone?
sa.model: We cannot win over a besetting sin by our own self-effort alone because the flesh has no power to defeat itself — self-control is a fruit the Spirit produces, not something the flesh manufactures by willpower. Victory depends on the Spirit's power working in us, not on our own resolve or strength.

sa.prompt: Use Proverbs 25:28 to describe a person who has no self-control.
sa.model: Proverbs 25:28 says, 'Whoever has no rule over his own spirit is like a city broken down, without walls.' A person with no self-control is left defenseless, wide open to every attack of temptation and sin, the way a city without walls lies exposed to any enemy that wishes to enter.

sa.prompt: What is the right foundation and motive for the disciplined life - grace or earning?
sa.model: The right foundation and motive for the disciplined life is grace, not earning. Salvation is the free gift of God, received by faith and settled at the cross; the disciplined life is not a way to win God's acceptance but the way a saved person lives out the grace already given, letting the Spirit produce what we cannot produce alone.
